item.title: 9th China International Import Expo opens in Shanghai
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
Despite rising uncertainties and headwinds in global trade, confidence of foreign companies in China remains unchanged, and this can be largely attributed to the country's continued efforts to advance higher-level opening-up and facilitate innovation, officials and top executives attending the 9th China International Import Expo said. That confidence is reflected in the record highs registered at this year's CIIE, which opened in Shanghai on Thursday and runs through Tuesday. Altogether, 4,142 overseas exhibitors are present at this year's business exhibition — the core commercial segment — more than in any previous editions. Furthermore, the total exhibition area exceeds 440,000 square meters for the first time, and more than 480 exhibits are expected to make their debut, another high. In his speech during Thursday's opening ceremony, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang said that various opening-up policies of China have been first introduced or better interpreted to the world through the CIIE. Quality products, innovative services, frontier technologies and application scenarios have all been extended worldwide through the expo. He said that amid a rapidly changing world economy, the consecutive CIIE editions are China's active moves to advocate an open world economy and strike a dynamic balance in world trade. Alexander De Croo, administrator of the United Nations Development Programme, said that while the world is facing rising pressures due to economic uncertainty, geopolitical tensions and climate change, the CIIE provides a crucial platform of dialogue and cooperation. The value of the CIIE lies not only in opening up the Chinese market, but also in the business ties that are created and tightened in the process, sharpening competitiveness of economies and elevating prosperity, he said. Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker agreed that dialogues addressing challenges and different perspectives openly and constructively form the very foundation of common prosperity. "Europe does not seek isolation. We seek engagement while also ensuring that our economic resilience and industrial capabilities remain strong," said Stocker, advocating deeper China-Austria cooperation in future-oriented technologies. Speaking at Thursday's event, Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema applauded China's green transition and digitalization. He said the zero-tariff treatment that China has comprehensively granted since May 1 to African countries that have diplomatic relations with China will help to build a community with a shared future for humanity. This year, the number of Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders attending the CIIE tops 300 for the first time. Caterpillar Inc, a United States-based construction and mining machinery manufacturer, is showcasing a range of digital technologies, energy solutions and services to address challenges across the infrastructure, mining and energy sectors. Alan Yang, the company's senior vice-president, considers the expo a valuable platform to connect with customers and key stakeholders, better understand their evolving needs and explore new opportunities. This year's expo is hosting over 2,000 first-time exhibitors, including Singapore-based Perennial Holdings. The group's project in Tianjin — China's first wholly foreign-owned tertiary comprehensive hospital — began operations in February 2025. A similar project is expected to open in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, at the end of this year, according to Zhai Lili, the company's head for brand promotion in China. Such progress testifies to China's institutional opening-up in trade of services, she said. Around 170 enterprises and 30 overseas organizations have participated in all nine editions of the CIIE. Swedish medical technology company Elekta is one of them. Gong Anming, president for China at Elekta, said the company is shifting from introducing global technologies to developing innovations locally and bringing Chinese clinical experience to international markets.

item.title: China's opening-up boon to global biz
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
With the global recovery still fragile and protectionism on the rise, China's resolve to open its door even wider will serve as a much-needed anchor of stability for the world economy and help foster a more balanced and inclusive pattern of growth for all, officials, experts and business leaders said on Thursday. The opportunities China offers the world now extend well beyond access to its vast market, with green development and technological innovation creating new avenues for shared growth, they said, calling on economies to move beyond bloc-based confrontation and jointly build a more open and inclusive world economy. "Shared growth and inclusive development should be at the heart of global economic rebalancing," said Mondher Mimouni, director of the Market Development Division at the International Trade Centre. Mimouni was speaking at a parallel session of the Hongqiao International Economic Forum, held alongside the ongoing 9th China International Import Expo in Shanghai. Jeffrey Sachs, a professor at Columbia University and former senior adviser to the United Nations, said the rebalancing is already visible in the shift of economic weight from the West toward Asia. "Asia is returning to the center of the world stage," Sachs said, adding that the region could account for 50 to 60 percent of the global economy in the coming years. The shift is not only geographic. It is also technological, Sachs said, as the world moves from the steam and oil eras toward green energy. China's strengths across clean-energy supply chains leave it well placed to lead the transition over the coming decades. That transition is also opening up development opportunities beyond China. Martin Jacques, a former senior fellow at the University of Cambridge, said China's cooperation in green technologies is creating new opportunities for industrialization elsewhere. "Rebalancing the global economy requires an open world economy built on mutual benefit and cooperation, rather than tariff barriers and decoupling," Jacques said. That call for greater market liberalization resonated with the World Openness Report 2026, which was unveiled at a separate news conference and symposium on world opening-up the same day. The report showed that China's openness index rose from 0.5891 in 1990 to 0.7551 in 2025, an increase of 28.18 percent and one of the strongest improvements worldwide. By contrast, the World Openness Index fell 1 percent year-on-year to 0.7453 in 2025, its steepest decline since 2016. "Even as global openness contracted sharply, China continued to open wider, moving up the rankings while maintaining a historically high level of openness," said Liao Fan, director of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of World Economics and Politics. Liu Ling, chief regional leader of Philips China, said, "We see a clear signal that China will further advance high-standard opening-up and share development opportunities with the world." Wang Xuekun, president of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, said innovation is emerging as another dividend of opening-up. "China's innovation is a source of dynamism for global development," Wang said, adding that the country is pursuing innovation through greater openness and working with global partners to address shared development challenges. zhangchenxu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: 'Mini-breaks' poised to boost tourism
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
China's tourism market is poised for a new wave of growth as students at primary and junior high schools will start their autumn breaks this month. Experts said the "minibreak" will help balance the seasonal fluctuation of the tourism market and promote an optimized paid vacation system. First implemented at certain provinces and cities in 2025, such as Sichuan and Zhejiang, more cities and regions have taken exploratory steps to develop their own autumn breaks for students this year. While the time for the autumn break varies from area to area, it mostly falls between late October and late November. For example, cities like Shenyang and Dandong in the northeastern province of Liaoning set the autumn break from Oct 29 to Nov 2, Taiyuan in Shanxi province from Nov 11 to Nov 13 and Xiamen in Fujian province from Nov 25 to Nov 27. Most of the autumn breaks last around three days, while some parents choose to extend it to a five-day holiday by connecting the break with the weekend. Tourism insiders believe that the mini-break will be a "shot in the arm" for the market, which is usually in low season after the weeklong National Day holiday which occurred in early October. Figures from Qunar, a travel portal, show that searches for products on "autumn break", "family trips" and "autumn viewing places" have risen by 220 percent at its platform so far compared with September and hotel bookings for trips in November registered a year-on-year rise of 50 percent. "There will be a month-long peak season for family trips till the end of December. Each weekend of November will see a travel peak and the market will see a boom around mid-November till the end of that month," Qunar said. The online travel agency Tuniu also gave encouraging reports, pointing out that family trips and educational tours to destinations with rich cultural or historical vibes have seen remarkable increases at its platform so far for the autumn breaks. It added that Shanghai, Beijing, Chengdu in Sichuan province and Sanya in Hainan province are gaining increasing popularity among autumn break goers. Wang Zhixiong, a manager from Tuniu who is in charge of the business in Chancheng district of Foshan, in Guangdong province, in the south, said that tours to Beijing for autumn scenery and historic scenic spots are the top choices for their customers. Trips to places with milder climates like Yunnan in Southwest China and Fujian in the nation's eastern part are also popular, where the travelers can enjoy mountainous views by hiking or experience cultural immersion by visiting handcraft workshops, he said. Wang Yiqi, a 40-year-old resident of Huzhou in the eastern province of Zhejiang, is preparing a four-day family trip to Beijing with his 10-year-old son around mid-November using the autumn break. "The break this year is from Nov 12 to Nov 16, connecting the weekend. It's a good season to visit Beijing, which is famous for its autumn views and historic spots. The break gives all of us — my son, my wife and me — a period to get away from academic burden or stressful work and go for an off-season trip," he said, adding that he will take his annual leave, as will his wife, to accompany their son to Beijing. He Jianhua, a researcher at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, told the China Business Journal that unlike public holidays, which have fixed dates, autumn breaks vary in timing from one area to another. This flexibility allows the minibreaks to help balance seasonal fluctuations in the tourism market. In March, the Government Work Report mentioned that local authorities are encouraged to decide and promote spring and autumn breaks and implement a paid vacation system so workers can travel off-peak.

item.title: Democracy sprouts from local elections
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
When President Xi Jinping cast his vote to elect deputies for Beijing's Xicheng district people's congress on Nov 5, 2021, he highlighted that the process was an embodiment of how the nation is run by the people. On that day, Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said that the election of deputies is fundamental to China's people's congress system. He emphasized that whole-process people's democracy relies on the integration of democratic elections with democratic consultations, decision-making, management and oversight. As democracy is a shared value of humanity, Xi stressed during a central conference on work related to people's congresses in 2021 that the key to a country's democracy lies in whether the people run the country, depending on if the people have the right to vote and, more important, if the people have the right to broad participation. There are many ways to achieve democracy, he said, calling for efforts to improve the system of people's congresses to ensure the realization of whole-process democracy in the country. China's people's congress system serves as the country's fundamental political system, based on the principle that all power belongs to the people. It is structured in multiple tiers, from the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature, down to congresses at the provincial, city, county and township levels. Deputies are elected at each level every five years. Between the elections, the consultative democracy continuously engages with the people through the congress system via means such as feedback loops, public opinion hotlines and community consultations. This year, a new round of elections for county and township deputies is underway nationwide. Wang Liguo, a resident of Fuzhoucheng town in Wafangdian, Liaoning province, cast his vote for township deputies on Oct 20. "This is my right as a voter, and it's our way, as citizens, to take part in governing the country," said Wang, one of over 700,000 voters in Wafangdian who went to polling stations across the city that day. "I approach voting seriously so that we can elect deputies to the people's congresses who truly represent the people." Jiao Hongchang, a law professor at China University of Political Science and Law in Beijing, said the election of county- and township-level lawmakers is the most direct expression of whole-process people's democracy, serving as the primary means by which the Constitution's electoral rights are realized. Under the Constitution, all citizens age 18 or older have the right to vote and run for election, regardless of ethnicity, race, gender, occupation, family background, religious beliefs, education level, property status or length of residence, except those legally deprived of political rights. According to China's electoral law, deputies to people's congresses at county and township levels are directly elected by voters, while deputies to people's congresses above the county level are elected by deputies from the next-lower level. Jiao said direct elections are the "starting point" of whole-process people's democracy. "They form the foundation for democratic elections, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight, vividly showcasing the authenticity, breadth and vitality of China's democracy," he said. Jiao added that the elected deputies serve as a bridge between State organs and the public. "The quality of deputy election affects governance ability and determines whether the power serves the people and reflects public opinion," he said. "The election of deputies to people's congresses is conducive to strengthening grassroots State power and modernizing local governance." In September, Song Rui, deputy secretary-general of the NPC Standing Committee, told a news conference that more than 1 billion voters nationwide will directly elect more than 2.6 million deputies to county and township people's congresses this year. He urged enhanced support for deputies in fulfilling their duties, maintaining close contact with the public, conveying their views and concerns, and helping to resolve practical issues. Li Ying, a resident of the Changsheng community in Gangdian subdistrict of Wafangdian, said that voting is a crucial part of political life. "Deputies represent us and express our concerns, so it's important for me to vote thoughtfully," she said after voting on Oct 20. "I hope the newly elected deputies will pay attention to our difficulties and genuinely help resolve our challenges." Mao Yuchong, a student at College of Science and Technology of China Three Gorges University in Yichang, Hubei province, recently cast his vote for the first time for deputies to the local people's congress. "I got up at 8 am to get ready," he said. "I'd only ever read about these elections in textbooks or seen them in films. Now I've experienced it myself. This is what democracy looks like." County and township authorities have implemented measures to make voter registration more inclusive and improve the voting process. In Liangxi district of Wuxi, Jiangsu province, an online platform was launched on WeChat to assist young residents and those living away from home in registering and discussing election-related matters. In remote mountain areas such as the towns of Wangyou and Xiantang in Guizhou province, staff members visited the homes of elderly voters and those with limited mobility to ensure they could exercise their right to vote. These efforts aim to enforce the Constitution and the electoral law, and uphold the people's role as the country's masters. Jiao, the professor, said that advancing the modernization of grassroots governance involves completing the new round of lawmaker elections at county and township levels, scientifically drawing constituency boundaries, protecting the voting rights of migrant populations, and rigorously reviewing deputy qualifications. "These are not only major political events, but also the shared expectations of the people," he said.

item.title: Wushu Olympics debut inspires Kenyans
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
On an open patch of ground beside a social hall in Kiambu County, north of Nairobi, about dozens of children punch, kick and hold their stances as their coach calls out instructions. "As we train, there is changquan (long fist), there is daoshu (broadsword), and gunshu (staff)," said Ngaruiya Njonge, president of the Kenya Kungfu Wushu Federation. "Also tai chi. There are a lot, actually." Wushu, a Chinese martial art gradually gaining popularity in Kenya, is spreading from a small circle of practitioners to public schools and clubs across the country. The sport marked a milestone at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, where it made its debut as an official medal sport. Held from Sunday to Tuesday, the competition brought together 47 athletes from 46 countries. In a country where, as Njonge put it, "many people know about only football", the growing interest in wushu is creating new opportunities for young people to explore a different sporting discipline. For some, the attraction begins with martial arts films featuring renowned Chinese action movie stars such as Jackie Chan, Jet Li and Donnie Yen. "We are impressed by their movies. Most of the kids admire them and want to learn kung fu," said Kennedy Murimi, a coach at Dagoretti Kungfu Club affiliated with the Kenya Kungfu Wushu Federation. Wushu's development in Kenya largely began with a small group of students introduced to kung fu by a Chinese master known as Muhir, who later left the country for Dubai, Murimi said. Njonge, who had practiced martial arts since childhood, was among about 15 Kenyans who trained under him, according to Murimi. In January 2000, Njonge established a club in Kiambu County, which later grew into the Kenya Kungfu Wushu Federation. In 2024, Njonge spent six months training at the Shaolin Temple in Henan province, earning a certificate that helped him secure opportunities to teach in public schools. "Going to Shaolin for me opens my door," he said. The federation now has 12 regional branches, works with 26 public schools and reaches about 6,000 students, Njonge said. One of its branches, led by Murimi, teaches about 300 students across several schools and at his club in Nairobi, where the youngest learners are just four years old. For Murimi, his wushu journey began under a Chinese master surnamed Huo about 15 years ago. He later trained at the Shaolin Temple before continuing his studies at Henan University of Technology. Murimi plans to return to China for a year to continue his training, with the intention of sharing the knowledge and skills he acquires with his students. International stage Kenyan practitioners have also begun gaining experience on the international stage. In February, young athletes attended a training camp in Egypt supported by the International Wushu Federation before going on to compete at the World Junior Wushu Championships in March. Among the young athletes hoping to build a future in the sport is 17-year-old Winfred Mukami. "My goal for wushu is to see myself rise higher, to achieve something big," she said. "I want to become a superstar in wushu." Despite its growing appeal among young Kenyans, wushu faces challenges in sustaining its expansion. As more children enroll, the demand for basic training equipment has increased, leaving shortages of uniforms, training weapons, and mats, Njonge said. The shortage of qualified coaches is another obstacle. Some clubs have limited access to Chinese instructors, while local coaches sometimes rely on online videos, including You-Tube, to learn new routines. But Njonge remains optimistic about its prospects. He is already looking ahead to the next international competition, with plans to prepare athletes for the World Wushu Championships that will be held in the Philippines next year. Nelly Ishimwe, 13, one of Murimi's students, was inspired by wushu's debut. She has her sights set on the international stage and hopes to represent Kenya at the Olympic Games one day. Shan Tianqing and Pei Tuo in Nairobi contributed to the story.

item.title: Guilin finds fresh ways to surprise
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
The flowing hair of women of the Red Yao ethnic group, the terraced slopes of Longji town, the limestone peaks lining the Lijiang River — these are the images that have long drawn travelers to Guilin, South China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. "The natural scenery of the Longji Rice Terraces is fascinating," says Mani Lamichhane, a senior director at the Nepal Tourism Board, who recently visited the city to see these celebrated sights. But he came away with more than memories of landscapes. He also praised the performances at the town's Huangluo Red Yao village and local residents' efforts to protect the environment while developing tourism. "I will definitely come back to Guilin," he says, adding that he believes travelers from around the world would enjoy the destination. Lamichhane was among more than 300 tourism professionals from across the Asia-Pacific region and beyond who gathered in Guilin in late October for the 20th UN Tourism/PATA Forum on Tourism Trends and Outlook. First hosted by the city in 2007, the forum explored emerging tourism trends and how artificial intelligence and digital technology are reshaping travel. Guilin has long attracted visitors with its karst landscape and terraced fields. Local tourism businesses now offer cultural activities on river cruises, in scenic areas and at hotels. On selected Lijiang River cruises, visitors can enjoy a Song Dynasty (960-1279) tea-making experience as the karst peaks drift past. On sightseeing boats in the Two Rivers and Four Lakes scenic area, performers present cai diao, a traditional folk opera that blends local songs, dance and comic acting. Drawing on everyday life, romance and local customs, the performances invite visitors to listen, join call-and-response activities and even try on costumes. Tang Hongling, general manager of the sales channel department at Guilin Tourism Corp, says the company has noticed a shift in the expectations of inbound visitors. "Visitors' needs are shifting from group sightseeing toward immersive experiences and deeper exploration," Tang says. Technology is also adding new dimensions to established attractions. At Yinzi Cave, also known as Silver Cave, 3D mapping projects images onto rock formations, including scenes inspired by A Panorama of Rivers and Mountains, a celebrated landscape painting by Song Dynasty artist Wang Ximeng. Colored lighting highlights the shapes and textures of the stalactites, while augmented-reality features offer visitors an interactive experience. At Zhujiang wharf on the Lijiang River, bilingual Chinese and English signs help visitors navigate the terminal, while Korean and Vietnamese guidance is available in key areas. The visitor center also provides multilingual translation devices and a dedicated service counter for inbound travelers. Hotels, too, are broadening their cultural offerings. At Shangri-La Guilin, general manager Chen Bihong says the hotel has introduced morning tai chi sessions and welcome performances featuring bamboo dance, a traditional dance practiced by ethnic groups in parts of southern China. It also hosts international meetings and provides accommodation and conference services for delegates. Chen says the hotel plans to expand cooperation with international businesses and organizations while developing more products that bring culture and tourism together.

item.title: China's progress a catalyst for new start, experts say
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
Former British lawmaker George Galloway recalled seeing metal so thin during a visit to a Chinese steel plant that it could be torn by hand. For him, it illustrated a transformation deserving closer attention: China is no longer simply supplying the world with T-shirts and toys, but increasingly with advanced technology. Galloway said China's progress offers lessons for other economies. What some portray as a danger is "the threat of a good example", he said in an interview during his recent visit to Beijing. China's industrial advances are giving other economies access to more affordable technology, new markets and opportunities to develop their own industries, political figures and scholars told China Daily. The term "China shock" is associated with research on job losses and slow adjustment in US communities exposed to rising imports from China. The label "China shock 2.0" is now used in debates over competition from Chinese exports in industries such as electric vehicles and solar energy. Several of the figures interviewed acknowledged that established industries outside China faced adjustment pressures. But they argued that viewing China's advances primarily as a threat risked overlooking the products, expertise and partnerships that could help other economies become more competitive.

item.title: Australia should withdraw from AUKUS
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
A five-month-long independent public inquiry into Australia's A$368 billion ($239 billion) AUKUS nuclear submarine program — led by former Labor minister Peter Garrett and former Australian defense force chief Chris Barrie — has delivered a Commissioner's Report, which judges the plan to be "the worst, riskiest and most costly defense decision ever made by an Australian government". The report, which was released on Wednesday, calls for the trilateral security agreement to be scrapped immediately, and a special commission to be established to investigate how Australia got into "this mess". In September 2021, Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States established the AUKUS "security" pact, which includes Australia's acquisition of technology for eight nuclear-powered submarines and aims to deepen cooperation on advanced military technologies such as cyber capabilities and quantum technologies. It was a deal to counter what the three nations perceived to be China's growing "assertiveness" in the "Indo-Pacific". Though the project was sold to the Australian people as a generational strategic necessity, the inquiry has concluded that it actually jeopardizes Australia's national sovereignty, ties the country to the US military bandwagon and endangers rather than enhances its security. "We should never allow an acquisition program like AUKUS to define our national security," Barrie noted. The so-called "security partnership" runs counter to Australia's national interests. Its staggering costs divert resources away from essential public needs, and it unnecessarily entangles Australia in geopolitical competition. It would be "madness" for Australia to take on a major country such as China, Barrie said. "It may serve the interests of the United States, but it would not serve ours." Indeed, AUKUS is by no means a mere "defense cooperation" initiative as claimed. Instead, it serves as an instrument for the US to advance bloc confrontation and fuel geopolitical rivalry across the Asia-Pacific. Through nuclear submarine cooperation, the US seeks to anchor Australia to its military planning, and beef up military deployments in the South Pacific and Southeast Asian waters. These moves threaten regional peace and stability. Australia is a non-nuclear-weapon state, and the AUKUS plan to transfer weapons-grade highly enriched uranium to power nuclear submarines raises high proliferation risks and presents grave hidden dangers for global nuclear governance. Such a move undermines the foundation of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and sets a dangerous precedent for other nations. Thus, the hegemony-driven arrangement contravenes the spirit and principles of the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty and the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon-Free Zone. It also risks triggering a regional arms race, casting a shadow of confrontation over the waters of the Asia-Pacific. It is encouraging that opposition to the AUKUS plan has been increasing in Australia. More and more Australian people are recognizing the significant risks associated with the project. The latest report reflects a concentrated voice of rational forces within Australian society. Facts suggest that blindly following an extraterritorial power in pursuit of enhanced military capability cannot deliver genuine security for Australia, and dependent military arrangements will only compromise Australia's strategic autonomy and increase the country's security risks. The Chinese government firmly opposes the AUKUS nuclear submarine program, calling it a "textbook case of nuclear proliferation", which risks sparking bloc confrontation in the region. While some neo-militarists in Japan increasingly long for US nuclear submarines to accelerate Japan's remilitarization, Australia has every reason to make the right choice. Withdrawing from the AUKUS program is the correct path for Australia to protect its own interests and help maintain regional peace.

item.title: Ningbo through world mayors' eyes: Building bridges between cities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
At the 2026 Global Mayors Dialogue · Ningbo, mayors from New Zealand, Lebanon and Mauritius shared their impressions of the city and reflected on the importance of friendly exchanges and mutual learning between cities. From cultural exchanges to youth engagement, cities are strengthening ties through open dialogue, deepening understanding and moving forward together.

item.title: What if we treat the world like a game?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
At the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit, let’s dive into world models that build lifelike virtual spaces. Here, you don’t need to fear failure! China Daily reporter Yan An meets Winston Ng, Singaporean student entrepreneur and 2026 WIC Global Youth Leader, who creates immersive virtual worlds. In these worlds, you can be a bus driver, firefighter or police officer. His team has also recreated a stunning digital Wuzhen, complete with indigo-dye workshops — just like the real world. The value of these virtual worlds lies in their ability to simulate extreme and hazardous scenarios, serving as a training ground for embodied intelligence. Humans can also learn and practice within these digital environments. For him, virtual worlds blend fun and learning. Virtual worlds will grow ever more fascinating. Yet what we strive for is always a better real world, the only place where you can have a decent meal.
